analysis.one_liner: Requires households with over $100 million in income or $1 billion in assets to pay tax on asset gains annually.
analysis.headline: The Billionaires Income Tax Act drew 19 Senate cosponsors — all Democrats plus one Independent — but the Finance Committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the wealthiest American households to pay income tax every year on the gains in their investment portfolios, the way workers pay tax on every paycheck. Today, someone whose wealth sits in stock that keeps rising owes no income tax on those gains until they sell — and, under the current 'stepped-up basis' rule, nothing at all if they hold the stock until death. The bill would tax tradable assets like stock at their year-end value, close the 'buy, borrow, die' strategy of borrowing against untaxed holdings to fund spending, and tax large gifts and inheritances of appreciated assets as if they had been sold. It applies only to households with more than $100 million in annual income or more than $1 billion in assets for three straight years.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday taxpayers, who pay income and payroll tax on every dollar of wages each year, gain because the federal burden would shift toward households that currently defer tax on rising asset values for decades — or escape it entirely at death. The bill's stated purpose is to make ultra-wealthy taxpayers pay annually 'just like working people do on their income from wages' [S2]. The bill does not specify how the new revenue would be spent.

how_it_helps.text: Requires 'applicable taxpayers' — individuals with more than $100 million in annual income ($50 million married filing separately) or more than $1 billion in covered assets — to recognize gain or loss on tradable assets each year as if they had been sold at fair market value [S2].

Closes the 'buy, borrow, die' strategies described in the bill's stated purpose, including the loophole that lets heirs sell inherited appreciated assets 'completely tax-free' under current stepped-up basis rules [S2].

Treats gifts, bequests, and transfers in trust of covered assets as a sale at fair market value, with exceptions for transfers between spouses, to charities, and to disability and cemetery funds [S2].

Modifies more than 30 additional tax provisions — including deferred compensation, like-kind exchanges, corporate stock transfers, and private placement life insurance — so that billionaires are taxed annually rather than deferring indefinitely [S2].

analysis.who_pays: A few hundred of the wealthiest households — those clearing $100 million in annual income or holding $1 billion or more in assets for three consecutive years — would owe tax on asset gains each year, including on gains they have not yet cashed in. Businesses they own would face new annual reporting of the value of their assets to those owners [S2].

drawbacks.text: Mark-to-market taxation means tax is owed on paper gains before anything is sold, so a household could owe tax in a year when it received little or no cash and might need to sell assets to pay the bill [S2].

Putting an annual value on illiquid holdings like private company stakes is difficult and contestable; the bill's rules rely heavily on the Treasury Secretary to set valuation methods and fill gaps by regulation [S2].
The bill would require private businesses held by these households to compute and report asset values to owner-taxpayers each year, a new compliance burden on the companies themselves [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: a tax code in which wages are taxed every year but billionaire wealth can compound untaxed until death is structurally tilted, and this bill directly attacks that gap. The honest costs are complexity and cash-flow risk — valuing private companies annually is genuinely hard, and taxing unsold gains can force sales in down markets. The bill tries to soften the first-year shock with a five-installment election and shields retirement accounts, spousal transfers, and charities. The narrow scope (roughly a few hundred households) limits both the revenue upside and the disruption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on November 30, 2023 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and the committee — chaired by the bill's own sponsor — never held a markup, hearing vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025 [S1][S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced S. 3367, the Billionaires Income Tax Act, on November 30, 2023 with 15 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced; that was the last action of record [S4].
The bill accumulated 19 cosponsors — 18 Democrats and 1 Independent — but never received a committee markup, hearing, or floor vote [S3].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and all bills not enacted died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with more than $100 million in income or $1 billion in assets keep the current rules: no tax on rising asset values until they sell, and nothing at all on gains passed to heirs at death. The wealth-planning industry keeps the 'buy, borrow, die' and estate-strategy business the bill targeted. Ordinary taxpayers continue to bear the annual income-tax burden the bill would have rebalanced.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor; Chair, Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Billionaires Income Tax Act and recruited 15 original cosponsors; as Finance Committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote [S1][S4].

for.name: Senate Democratic and Independent cosponsors (18 D, 1 I)
for.role: 19 Senate cosponsors, including Sens. Warren, Sanders, Brown, Casey, Whitehouse, Fetterman, and Markey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the cosponsors moved it out of committee [S3].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (never scheduled a markup or vote)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further recorded action for the remainder of the Congress [S4].

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Senate Republican cosponsored the bill, and the party's members uniformly opposed taxing unrealized gains as double taxation.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent; no Republican signed on, and no vote ever took place that would have shown the chamber's actual split.

industries.industry: Households with over $100 million in income or $1 billion in assets
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to defer tax on rising asset values for decades and to pass appreciated assets to heirs untaxed. Their interest in the current rules runs against ordinary taxpayers, who pay tax on every year's wages.

industries.industry: Private wealth management, tax advisory, and estate-planning firms
industries.note: Strategies like 'buy, borrow, die', like-kind exchanges of high-value assets, private placement life insurance, and stepped-up-basis estate planning — the bill's explicit targets [S2] — are the products these firms sell to the ultra-wealthy. Shutting them down shrinks that business.

industries.industry: Private businesses held by billionaire owners
industries.note: Companies owned by applicable taxpayers would face new annual reporting duties: valuing their covered assets and reporting each owner's share of gains and losses to the owner [S2]. No tax is imposed on the entity itself, but the compliance burden is real and falls on the businesses.
